Only when float cannot absorb the gap does the question become one of extra funding, a later finish or less scope, and those decisions belong to the people who own them. Reserves cover risk; they are not a way of reconciling a known funding profile.
questions.mindset: Use the room the plan already holds before asking anyone to change its limits.

questions.stem: A regional newspaper has funded a new team to build a subscription app, and the first sprint starts in a week. The editor-in-chief, acting as product owner, has a clear aim of converting print readers to digital subscriptions and a long list of feature ideas. The IT director would like a complete requirements specification and a six-month delivery schedule before the team writes any code. Which two things are needed before the first sprint starts?

options.text: A product goal stating the outcome the app is meant to achieve for print readers, agreed between the editor-in-chief and the team.
options.rationale: The goal is what lets the team and the product owner judge every later choice. It is cheap to agree now and is the one thing the team cannot sensibly start without.

options.text: An ordered backlog whose top items are refined enough for the team to plan its first sprint, with the rest left at a coarser level.
options.rationale: The first sprint needs only enough refined work to plan it. Leaving later items coarse accepts that they will change as the team and readers learn what works.

options.text: A complete requirements specification signed off by the IT director, so that the team builds against an agreed and stable scope from the start.
options.rationale: The candidate applies predictive entry criteria to adaptive work. Detailing every requirement now spends effort on ideas that early reader feedback is likely to change or remove.

options.text: A six-month schedule allocating each idea on the list to a specific sprint, so that stakeholders can see when every feature will arrive.
options.rationale: It plans in detail far beyond the horizon the team can see. The candidate mistakes a sprint-by-sprint allocation for a forecast, when the team has no delivery history to base one on.

options.text: A velocity figure for the new team, estimated in advance from the size of the list, so that a release date can be committed to now.
options.rationale: Velocity is observed, not estimated in advance. The candidate wants a commitment the evidence cannot yet support, and a date fixed now would rest on a guess.

questions.explanation: Adaptive planning needs just enough to start: a goal that tells everyone what success looks like, and enough ordered, refined work to plan the first iteration. Detail is added progressively as the work and the team's understanding develop, and forecasts come from observed delivery rather than predicted rates. Demanding full specification before starting moves the cost of change to the moment when the least has been learned.
questions.mindset: Plan enough to start well, and let the detail arrive with the learning.

questions.stem: A social care provider's product team has a flat backlog of 180 user stories for an app that schedules home-care visits. After three sprints, managers and carers say they cannot tell what the first release will let them do, and the product owner is struggling to decide which stories make a usable first version. Which two actions should you suggest?

options.text: Run a story-mapping workshop with carers and managers that lays the stories out along the steps of a carer's working day.
options.rationale: Arranging stories along the user's journey shows how they combine into something a carer can actually do, and exposes the steps that have no stories at all.

options.text: Agree a goal for the first release, then slice the map to the thinnest set of stories that lets a carer complete a full day's visits.
options.rationale: A release goal gives the product owner a test for what belongs in the first version, and an end-to-end slice delivers something usable rather than a finished part.

options.text: Ask the team to estimate all 180 stories in a single session, so that the product owner can see the total size of the work before choosing.
options.rationale: The candidate treats a structure problem as a sizing problem. Knowing the total size of a flat list still does not show which stories make a usable release.

options.text: Group the backlog by technical component, such as scheduling engine, mobile screens and reporting, so that each part can be released in turn.
options.rationale: Component releases are easy for the team to plan but give carers nothing they can use until every part is done. The candidate organises around the system rather than the user.

options.text: Ask managers and carers to rank all 180 stories in an online survey, and order the backlog by the combined scores so their priorities show directly.
options.rationale: Ranking stories in isolation produces a popular list, not a coherent release. The candidate also hands the ordering decision to a survey rather than to the accountable product owner.

questions.explanation: A flat list hides how stories combine into something a user can do, so release planning stalls even when every item is well written. Arranging the work along the user's journey makes the gaps and the smallest end-to-end slice visible, and a release goal gives a test for what belongs in that slice. Sizing or ranking items one by one adds information without adding the structure that the release decision needs.
questions.mindset: Plan releases around what a user can do from start to finish, not around a list of parts.

questions.stem: You are planning an insurer's move of 600 staff into a refurbished six-floor office. The draft schedule finishes three weeks after the old lease ends, and the sponsor has asked you to look for logic the project can change before considering any extra cost. Which two dependencies are the strongest candidates to challenge?

options.text: IT cabling on each floor waits until carpets are laid on all six floors, because that is how the fit-out contractor usually sequences its work.
options.rationale: This is preferred practice, not a necessity. Cabling can follow carpets floor by floor, and that overlap is the project's own decision to make.

options.text: Furniture assembly starts only after the whole building has been repainted, following the facilities team's practice on its previous office move.
options.rationale: Habit from the last move sets this link, not any physical or legal need. Assembly can begin on floors that are already painted while painting continues elsewhere.

options.text: Power cannot be switched on to the new electrical installation until the certified inspection has been completed and its certificate issued.
options.rationale: The candidate looks for time in a mandatory dependency. Energising an uncertified installation breaches safety regulations, so this link is not the project's to change.

options.text: Floor finishes cannot be laid until the new screed has dried to the moisture level stated in the flooring manufacturer's warranty terms.
options.rationale: This is a physical and contractual dependency. Laying finishes early risks failure and voids the warranty, so the candidate would be trading three weeks for a defect.

options.text: Removal vans can use the loading bay only on the weekend dates allocated by the landlord's building management, as set out in the lease.
options.rationale: This is an external dependency controlled by the landlord. It may be negotiable, but only with someone else's agreement, so it is not logic the project can change itself.

questions.explanation: Schedule logic comes in kinds: mandatory dependencies arise from law, physics or contract terms; external ones are set by parties outside the project; discretionary ones reflect preferred practice. When a schedule must be shortened without extra cost, discretionary logic is the first place to look, because the project can change it by its own decision, often by letting work overlap area by area. Challenging mandatory or external links either fails or depends on someone else agreeing.
questions.mindset: Find out which links in the logic are choices before treating the schedule as fixed.

questions.stem: A veterinary practice group's product team is building an appointment booking app in two-week sprints. Match each planning decision to the person or group who should make it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Online repeat prescriptions and video consultations cannot both fit in the next release, and someone must decide which comes first.
With two people on leave, someone must decide how many of the refined backlog items can realistically be finished in the coming sprint.
After the quarterly review, someone must decide whether the group keeps funding the app for another year or moves the money elsewhere.

options.text: The product owner
options.rationale: Choosing between two valuable features is a judgement about value and order, which is what the product owner is accountable for.

options.text: The developers on the team
options.rationale: How much fits in a sprint depends on capacity and on how the work will be done, which only the people doing it can judge. A forecast imposed from outside is a wish.

options.text: The executive sponsor who holds the budget
options.rationale: Continuing or stopping investment is a funding decision. The sponsor owns the money and the business case, so the decision sits with them, informed by what the review showed.

options.text: The delivery lead who facilitates the team's planning
options.rationale: Not used. The delivery lead runs the planning events and makes the decisions easier to take, which is why candidates often hand them all three, but facilitating a decision is not owning it.

questions.explanation: Adaptive planning splits decisions by the knowledge they need: what to build next is a value judgement for the person accountable for the product, how much fits in an iteration is a capacity judgement for the people who will do the work, and whether to keep investing is a funding judgement for whoever owns the budget. Facilitators make these decisions easier; they do not take them. Routing each decision to its owner keeps the plan credible, because each part of it is backed by the person who must stand behind it.
questions.mindset: Send each planning decision to the person who holds both the knowledge and the accountability for it.

questions.stem: While integrating the plan for a 120-home housing development, you collect several items from the workstream leads. Match each item to the planning document where it should be recorded first. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The groundworks schedule is built on the supplier's verbal statement that precast foundation beams will arrive in week 14, which nobody has confirmed in writing.
The council may restrict working hours when it decides on the construction management plan next month, which would lengthen the build.
The temporary access road flooded on Monday, and concrete deliveries cannot reach plots 1 to 30 until it has been repaired.

options.text: Assumption log
options.rationale: The schedule treats the week-14 delivery as true without proof. Recording it as an assumption puts it on the list to be validated, and if validation shows doubt it can then be raised as a risk.

options.text: Risk register
options.rationale: The restriction is an uncertain future event that would affect the schedule if it happened. It needs an owner, an assessment and a planned response before the council decides.

options.text: Issue log
options.rationale: The flood has already happened and is stopping work now. It needs an owner and an action to resolve it, not an assessment of whether it might occur.

options.text: Change log
options.rationale: Not used. A change log records requests to alter an approved baseline. Resolving one of these items might later lead to a change request, but recording it there first skips the assessment that decides whether a change is needed.

questions.explanation: Planning information is sorted by how certain it is and when it bites: something treated as true without proof is an assumption to validate, an uncertain future event that would affect objectives is a risk, and something already happening that needs action is an issue. The category decides the next step, whether that is validation, a planned response or immediate resolution, and a change request follows only if dealing with the item would alter an approved baseline.
questions.mindset: Classify by what is known and when, because the category decides the response.

questions.stem: A pet-food manufacturer's hybrid programme builds a new packing hall predictively, while an agile team builds a trade ordering portal for retailers. The steering group asks you three questions. Complete each sentence with the evidence the answer should rest on. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Asked when the packing hall will be ready for production trials, you should answer from
Asked when retailers will be able to place and track orders online, you should answer from
Asked what the programme as a whole will cost to complete, you should answer from

options.text: the critical path of the hall's resource-loaded schedule, together with its float
options.rationale: The hall is planned predictively, so its finish comes from its scheduled logic. The float on the path tells the steering group how much slippage the trials date can absorb.

options.text: a range forecast from the portal team's measured velocity against its remaining ordered backlog
options.rationale: The portal's evidence is its observed delivery rate against what remains. Giving a range shows the steering group how uncertain that forecast honestly is.

options.text: the hall's remaining cost baseline plus the portal team's cost per sprint over its forecast range
options.rationale: Each workstream is costed on the basis it is funded: the hall against its baseline, the portal as a team running for a forecast number of sprints. Adding the two gives a range the steering group can plan against.

options.text: a single portal date produced by converting its remaining story points into hours in the master schedule
options.rationale: Not used. Converting points into hours gives a precise-looking date with none of the evidence behind it. It is tempting because it makes the portal look like the hall, but it hides the uncertainty the steering group needs to see.

options.text: the workstream leads' own estimates of percentage complete, averaged across the programme
options.rationale: Not used. Self-reported percentages are the least reliable progress measure in either approach, and averaging a building with a software product blends two measures that mean different things.

questions.explanation: Each kind of work produces its own forecasting evidence: a predictive build is forecast from its scheduled logic and float, an adaptive team from its observed delivery rate against what remains, and cost from the basis on which each part is funded. An integrated plan combines those forecasts without converting one into the other's units, and shows the adaptive ones as ranges because that is what the evidence supports. Forcing one method onto both produces figures that look comparable and are not.
questions.mindset: Answer each question from the evidence that kind of work actually produces.

questions.stem: A language-learning app team has 260 points left in its release backlog. Over its last six two-week sprints, velocity ranged from 31 to 40 points. The marketing director wants a forecast to plan the launch campaign. Assuming the scope stays as it is, work out the forecast range in whole sprints.

blanks.label: Fewest whole sprints needed, at the highest observed velocity
blanks.rationale: 260 ÷ 40 = 6.5. A part-sprint still needs a whole sprint, so at the best observed velocity the release needs 7 sprints.

blanks.label: Most whole sprints needed, at the lowest observed velocity
blanks.rationale: 260 ÷ 31 = 8.39, which rounds up to 9 sprints. This is the slow end of the range, which a campaign that cannot move should be planned around.

blanks.label: Width of the window between those two outcomes, in weeks
blanks.rationale: The range runs from 7 to 9 sprints, a difference of 2 sprints. At two weeks per sprint that is a 4-week window for the launch.

questions.explanation: An adaptive release forecast is a range built from the team's own observed velocity, not a single date from its average. Dividing the remaining work by the highest and lowest recent rates, and rounding up to whole iterations, shows stakeholders both the likely window and how wide it is. Planning a dependent event such as a campaign then becomes a choice about how much of that window to accept, made by the person who owns the event.
questions.mindset: Give the range the evidence supports, so others can plan with its width in view.

questions.stem: Your £2.1 million extension to a secondary school is scheduled to finish one week after the autumn term starts, and the governors have approved extra spending to recover that week. There is one critical path, and no other path has less than two weeks of float. Each box shows an activity, its total float and the cost of shortening it by one week. Select the activity to shorten first.

graphic.title: Five schedule activities with total float and one-week compression cost
graphic.caption: Select an activity. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Foundations — float 0 weeks — £18,000 to shorten by one week
regions.rationale: Foundations are on the critical path, so shortening them would recover the week, but at nearly twice the cost of another critical activity. The candidate stops at the first critical activity rather than comparing them.

regions.label: Steel frame — float 0 weeks — £9,500 to shorten by one week
regions.rationale: It is on the critical path and is the cheapest critical activity to shorten. With every other path holding at least two weeks of float, one week taken out here comes straight off the finish date.

regions.label: Roof covering — float 0 weeks — £12,000 to shorten by one week
regions.rationale: Roofing is critical and would recover the week, but it costs £2,500 more than another critical activity that does the same job. The candidate chooses a valid option without checking for a cheaper one.

regions.label: External landscaping — float 4 weeks — £3,000 to shorten by one week
regions.rationale: It is cheap to shorten, but with four weeks of float it is not driving the finish. The candidate picks the lowest price without checking whether the activity is on the critical path, and the term-start date would not move.

regions.label: Furniture delivery — float 2 weeks — £1,500 to shorten by one week
regions.rationale: The cheapest option of all, but its float means shortening it recovers nothing. Spending money on non-critical work is the classic crashing error: it buys time where none is needed.

questions.explanation: Crashing buys time with money, so the purchase has to be made where it shortens the project and at the lowest price per unit of time. That means looking only at activities on the critical path, comparing their cost to shorten, and starting with the cheapest, while checking that no other path becomes critical as the compression proceeds. Cheap compression off the critical path buys nothing, and expensive compression on it wastes money that a cheaper critical activity would have saved.
questions.mindset: Spend schedule money only where it moves the finish, and there at the lowest price.
